title: D&I4DBT Class 4 – Network Society & Digital Transformation
subtitle: EPITA – Design & Innovation for Digital Business Transformation | Social (non-technical) drivers, Network Properties, Regulation

questions.question: Which term describes technologies that have relatively higher potential to bring about widespread economic and social change, such as AI and Machine Learning?
options: General Purpose Technologies
Infrastructural Technologies
Disruptive Technologies
Platform Technologies
questions.explanation: General Purpose Technologies (GPT) are defined as technologies with higher potential to bring about transformative change. AI and ML are cited as examples (Thesis #5). Infrastructural technologies like IoT and Blockchain are explicitly contrasted with GPTs in Thesis #6.

questions.question: According to Thesis #6, what distinguishes AI/ML from other infrastructural technologies like IoT or Blockchain?
options: AI/ML encompasses activities and processes normally performed by humans, such as decision-making
AI/ML is exclusively used for data storage and retrieval
AI/ML requires more hardware infrastructure than IoT
AI/ML operates independently of any social context
questions.explanation: Thesis #6 states that AI/ML's potential encompasses human activities like decision-making, increasing 'human activity embeddedness in technology.' This is what sets it apart from IoT and Blockchain, which do not inherently replace human cognitive tasks at the same scale.

questions.question: Thesis #7 raises which fundamental question in the era of AI-driven Digital Transformation?
options: Which activities should remain human and which can be delegated to AI
How to maximize algorithmic efficiency in production lines
Whether blockchain can replace traditional financial systems
How to reduce the cost of digital infrastructure
questions.explanation: Thesis #7 explicitly asks which activities should continue to be performed by humans versus delegated to AI. This reflects the ethical and strategic dimension of AI adoption, beyond purely technical questions of cost or efficiency.

questions.question: The concept of 'human agency' in the context of digital transformation refers to:
options: Humans making decisions and enacting them on the world, independently
The capacity of algorithms to act and make decisions with limited human intervention
The tendency to view technology as central to addressing complex social issues
The ability of platforms to predict user behavior from past data
questions.explanation: Human agency entails the claim that humans make decisions and enact them on the world, independent of whether this is deterministic or through free will. Algorithmic agency (option B) and technocentrism (option C) are distinct concepts defined separately in the course material.

questions.question: Technocentrism is defined as:
options: The tendency to view technology as a central component for addressing complex social issues and driving transformative change
The process by which algorithms replace human workers in production
The study of how digital networks reshape political power structures
A framework for measuring the economic impact of new technologies
questions.explanation: Technocentrism is the tendency to view technology as a central component for addressing complex social issues and driving transformative changes. It is one of three definitions introduced as a starting point in Class 4, alongside human agency and algorithmic agency.

questions.question: In the historical model presented (Society, Economy, and Technology), what role did technology play in a pre-digital society?
options: A means for reaching goals: building infrastructure to support society's needs
The primary driver of cultural values and social norms
An autonomous force reshaping markets independently of human intent
A tool for surveillance and social control
questions.explanation: In the pre-digital model (Phase I), technology served as a means for reaching goals — building infrastructure like railroads, electricity, and telecommunications — in support of society's needs. It was not yet an autonomous or dominant force shaping society itself.

questions.question: Which internal factor influencing technology diffusion relates to the ability of different technologies or systems to work together?
options: Interoperability and compatibility
Cultural reluctance
Organizational factors
Social amplification
questions.explanation: Interoperability and compatibility are listed as internal factors influencing technology diffusion. Cultural reluctance and social amplification are external factors, while organizational factors (individual vs. collective action) are also external.

questions.question: Which of the following is an EXTERNAL factor in technology diffusion?
options: Social factors — amplification of positive or harmful social phenomena
Modularity of component technologies
Stability and safety of the technology
Range of possible applications
questions.explanation: Social factors (amplification of phenomena), cultural factors, and organizational factors are all external factors. Modularity, stability/safety, and range of applications are internal factors pertaining to the technology itself.

questions.question: The Arab Spring (2010–2012) is frequently cited in digital transformation studies primarily because:
options: Social media and digital technologies enabled collective activism that circumvented state-operated media
It demonstrated that algorithmic recommendation systems can prevent political conflict
Governments used AI to predict and suppress protests before they occurred
It showed that digital literacy was insufficient in developing countries
questions.explanation: The Arab Spring showed how social media allowed citizens to circumvent state media for collective activism. The course frames it as an early large-scale illustration of social digital transformation — both its beneficial potential (collective action) and risks.

questions.question: Cambridge Analytica (2018 scandal) is cited as an example of which phenomenon?
options: The use of personal data harvested from social platforms to influence political outcomes
A government regulator successfully enforcing data privacy law
A tech company developing an open-source AI recommendation system
Corporate whistleblowing leading to voluntary platform reform
questions.explanation: Cambridge Analytica was accused of harvesting the personal data of 87 million Facebook users to build psychographic profiles used in political campaigning. It illustrates the harmful social consequences of data misuse by a commercial entity, not regulatory success or voluntary reform.

questions.question: The 2020 US House of Representatives inquiry found that Facebook's monopoly power was 'firmly entrenched' partly because of:
options: Strategic acquisitions and copying competitor products, with Onavo providing early warning signals
Exclusive government contracts that blocked rival social platforms
Superior algorithmic recommendations unavailable to competitors
A legal framework that actively protected social media monopolies
questions.explanation: The inquiry found that Facebook used strategic acquisitions (e.g., Instagram, WhatsApp) and copied rivals, while Onavo — a data analytics firm it acquired — helped identify rising competitors as 'early bird warning' signals. Options B, C, and D are not supported by the course material.

questions.question: The 2023 'Pause Giant AI Experiments' open letter called for:
options: All AI labs to pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4
A permanent ban on large language models in educational settings
Mandatory open-sourcing of all AI models above a certain parameter threshold
The creation of an international AI governance body under UN oversight
questions.explanation: The letter, published by the Future of Life Institute in March 2023, called for a 6-month pause on training AI systems more powerful than GPT-4, citing risks including AI-generated propaganda, extreme automation, and societal loss of control. It did not call for a permanent ban or specific international governance structure.

questions.question: Herding in humans is defined as:
options: The alignment of thoughts or behaviors of individuals in a group through local interactions rather than centralized coordination
The adoption of technology by a dominant social class that then influences others
Centralized media campaigns that shift public opinion simultaneously
The process by which prices converge in competitive markets through supply and demand
questions.explanation: Herding is defined as alignment of thoughts or behaviors through local interactions, not centralized coordination. This is key: it is a bottom-up, emergent phenomenon, not a top-down campaign (option C) or market price mechanism (option D).

questions.question: Mark Granovetter's contribution to the study of herding and social networks concerns:
options: The role of weak ties in social networks and the transmission of information
The mathematical modeling of epidemic spread in urban populations
The economic theory of rational expectations in financial markets
The impact of strong hierarchical ties on organizational performance
questions.explanation: Granovetter (1973) demonstrated the role of 'weak ties' in social networks, showing that novel information flows primarily through weak ties, not strong ties. His work is cited in the context of social interdependence analysis and herding.

questions.question: In the context of social digital transformation, which pairing correctly matches a harmful social phenomenon with its digital manifestation?
options: Misinformation → fake news and disinformation online
Shared knowledge → conspiracy theories on social platforms
Mass movements → crowdsourcing for commercial gain
Global mobilization → hate speech moderation algorithms
questions.explanation: Misinformation maps to fake news and disinformation — both are listed together as harmful social phenomena amplified by digital transformation. Shared knowledge and mass movements are listed as beneficial phenomena, not harmful ones.

questions.question: Boullier (2023) identifies several types of social propagation. Which type corresponds to the spread of scientific theories across research communities?
options: Propagation of ideas (Science Paradigms)
Propagation of values (Social Cohesion)
Propagation of information (Consensus/Dissension)
Mass propagations (Herding/Migrations)
questions.explanation: Boullier's framework maps types of propagation to phenomena: ideas map to science paradigms, values to social cohesion, information to consensus/dissension, and mass propagations to herding/migrations. Virus propagation maps to epidemics.

questions.question: John Maynard Keynes is cited in the context of herding because he identified:
options: The influence of human emotions ('animal spirits') on economic agents
The mathematical relationship between social network size and economic output
The tendency of markets to self-correct without external intervention
The role of strong institutional hierarchies in stabilizing economic systems
questions.explanation: Keynes identified 'animal spirits' — human emotions influencing economic decision-making — as an example of herding in economics. This is contrasted with rational agent models and illustrates that social influence operates in economic contexts as well.

questions.question: According to Manuel Castells, what distinguishes a 'network society' from earlier forms of social organization based on networks?
options: Social networks that process and manage information using micro-electronic technologies
The size of the network exceeding national borders for the first time
The shift from informal networks to legally codified organizational structures
The replacement of market mechanisms by network-based exchange protocols
questions.explanation: Castells specifies that the network society is not just about social networks (which have existed for millennia) but about networks that process and manage information using micro-electronic technologies. This technological dimension is the distinguishing feature.

questions.question: In Powell's (1990) framework, what is the primary mode of conflict resolution in hierarchies?
options: Administrative authority (fiat) through detailed contracts
Relational and recurrent contracts with joint negotiation and reciprocity
Market norms and courts or legal systems
Reputation-based mediation through peer review
questions.explanation: In hierarchies, conflict is resolved through administrative authority (fiat) and detailed contracts. Networks rely on relational/recurrent contracts and reciprocity, while markets use market norms and legal systems (courts). These are key distinguishing attributes in Powell's framework.

questions.question: In Powell's (1990) framework, how are individual preferences characterized in market-based coordination?
options: Independent ('arm's length'), with no relational ties between transacting parties
Dependent on the authority of a central executive
Interdependent, shaped by reciprocal relationships within a community
Fixed by regulatory constraints and pricing mechanisms
questions.explanation: In markets, individual preferences are independent ('arm's length'): each transaction is discrete and atomic. In hierarchies, preferences are dependent on central authority; in networks, they are interdependent through reciprocal relationships.

questions.question: According to Van Alstyne (1997), the mode of influence/control in networks is based on:
options: Expertise or reputation
Status or rules
Pricing mechanisms and persuasion
Administrative procedures and bureaucracy
questions.explanation: In networks, control/authority is based on expertise or reputation. In hierarchies, it is based on status or rules; in markets, on persuasion via pricing mechanisms. This reflects the decentralized, trust-based nature of network coordination.

questions.question: Which organizational form has boundaries characterized as 'flexible and permeable'?
options: Networks
Hierarchies
Markets
Bureaucracies
questions.explanation: Networks have flexible and permeable boundaries, with strong and weak, often dynamic ties. Hierarchies have fixed, rigid boundaries with strong stable associations. Markets have discrete, atomic boundaries with arm's-length, one-time ties.

questions.question: The 'diffusion of a networking logic' according to Castells substantially modifies outcomes in which domains?
options: Production, experience, power, and culture
Pricing, competition, regulation, and innovation
Manufacturing, logistics, finance, and retail
Hardware, software, connectivity, and security
questions.explanation: Castells states that 'the diffusion of a networking logic substantially modifies the operation and outcomes in processes of production, experience, power, and culture.' This is a broad sociological claim, not limited to economic or technical domains.

questions.question: Which coordination mechanism typically requires external intervention through regulation to function properly?
options: Markets
Hierarchies
Networks
Communities
questions.explanation: Markets may require external intervention through regulation because individual preferences are independent and there is no built-in governance mechanism. Hierarchies have internal authority; networks have built-in governance through reciprocity and trust.

questions.question: A market is defined in the course as a mechanism where:
options: Exchange takes place as a result of buyers and sellers engaging through prices, establishing value
Individuals are arranged according to their relative importance in a social hierarchy
Resources are allocated through reciprocal relationships among members of a community
Information is processed and distributed through micro-electronic networks
questions.explanation: A market is defined as a composition of systems and institutions whereby parties engage in exchange, with prices of goods and services being established. Option B describes a hierarchy; option C describes a network; option D describes the network society concept.

questions.question: Social capital, as a sociological concept, relates a person's network position or ties to outcomes such as:
options: Power, leadership, mobility, employment, and entrepreneurship
Algorithmic ranking, audience size, and digital reach
Regulatory compliance, legal standing, and contractual rights
Hardware ownership, software licensing, and platform access
questions.explanation: Social capital relates network ties or position to outcomes including power, leadership, mobility, employment, individual performance, and entrepreneurship. It is a sociological concept about the value of one's relationships, not a digital metrics concept.

questions.question: A structural hole, as defined by Ronald Burt (1992), is:
options: A gap between two individuals who have complementary sources of information, bridged by a third party
A missing node in a scale-free network that prevents information flow between hubs
A regulatory gap exploited by tech companies to avoid antitrust enforcement
The absence of weak ties between geographically distant communities
questions.explanation: A structural hole is a gap between two individuals with complementary information. An individual who builds a bridge between these groups is in a privileged position to transfer or gatekeep valuable information. This is Burt's (1992) concept of social capital through network position.

questions.question: Stanley Milgram's 1967 experiment established that the maximum number of intermediaries between any two randomly selected people in the world is:
options: 5 intermediaries (6 degrees of separation)
3 intermediaries (4 degrees of separation)
10 intermediaries (11 degrees of separation)
19 intermediaries (20 degrees of separation)
questions.explanation: Milgram established that the longest path between any 2 people involves 5 intermediaries — hence '6 degrees of separation' (counting both endpoints). The path is X–1–2–3–4–5–Y. The figure of 19 refers to the 'diameter' of the web (Albert, Barabasi), not Milgram's social experiment.

questions.question: The 'Small Worlds' phenomenon in social networks results in:
options: Strangers being linked by a short chain of acquaintances
All nodes in a network having identical numbers of connections
The emergence of a single dominant hub connecting all other nodes
The complete disconnection of local communities from global networks
questions.explanation: Small Worlds refers to the observation — triggered by Milgram's experiment — that strangers are linked by a surprisingly short chain of acquaintances. It does not imply uniform degree distribution (option B) or a single dominant hub (option C).

questions.question: Strong ties in a social network are characterized by:
options: Frequent interaction between people who know each other very well (family, old friends, co-workers)
Rare, informal interaction with distant acquaintances who provide novel information
Connections between individuals who have never interacted but share indirect paths
Algorithmic connections generated by platform recommendation engines
questions.explanation: Strong ties are between people who know each other very well and interact frequently — family, old friends, boss, co-workers. Weak ties (option B) are acquaintances with infrequent, informal interaction. Invisible ties are between people who know each other by sight without significant interaction.

questions.question: According to Granovetter (1973), why do weak ties carry greater social value than strong ties for job searching?
options: Acquaintances move in different social circles, providing access to novel information not already known
Strong ties are legally restricted from sharing professional opportunities under labor law
Weak ties have greater algorithmic visibility on professional networking platforms
Close friends tend to have more formal education, but are less willing to share contacts
questions.explanation: Granovetter showed that close friends move in the same circles and share overlapping information. Acquaintances (weak ties) move in different circles, bringing novel information — including job leads. This is why weak ties are the 'likeliest to help finding a job.' Options B, C, and D introduce factors not present in Granovetter's argument.

questions.question: Invisible ties in a social network refer to connections between people who:
options: Know each other by sight and meet infrequently, without significant interaction
Have never met but are connected through more than 5 intermediaries
Are members of the same online community but have never met offline
Share professional credentials but have no personal relationship
questions.explanation: Invisible ties are defined as connections between people who know each other by sight and meet infrequently without significant interaction — like a commuting neighbor or a newspaper stand owner. They are distinct from both strong ties (high frequency, deep relationship) and weak ties (acquaintances with some interaction).

questions.question: A person who occupies a structural hole — bridging two distinct, disconnected social groups — is said to be in what kind of position?
options: A privileged position to transfer or gatekeep valuable information between groups
A vulnerable position due to conflicting loyalties from both groups
A neutral position with equal information access from all network nodes
A regulated position subject to data protection obligations
questions.explanation: Burt's theory holds that the broker occupying a structural hole — bridging two groups — is privileged: they control the flow of information between groups, giving them power or advantage. This is the essence of social capital derived from network position.

questions.question: The Pareto Principle (80-20 rule) is a manifestation of which mathematical distribution?
options: A power-law distribution
A normal (Gaussian) distribution
A uniform distribution
A binomial distribution
questions.explanation: The Pareto Principle is a power-law: 80% of outcomes arise from 20% of causes. Power-laws appear in wealth distribution, network connectivity, and many social phenomena. Normal distributions are symmetric and do not exhibit the long-tail 'winner-takes-most' property of the Pareto distribution.

questions.question: In a scale-free network, nodes with a disproportionately high number of connections compared to the average are called:
options: Hubs
Bridges
Cliques
Brokers
questions.explanation: In scale-free networks (Albert, Barabasi, 1999), nodes with higher degrees (more connections) are called 'hubs.' Bridges connect separate clusters; cliques are fully connected subgraphs; brokers occupy structural holes. Hubs are the defining structural feature of scale-free networks.

questions.question: Preferential attachment in scale-free networks is also known as the 'Matthew effect' because:
options: Nodes that already have more connections continue to attract more connections — 'the rich get richer'
Early adopters of a technology gain permanent regulatory protection from new entrants
Users who generate the most data are compensated proportionally for their contributions
The most popular content on a platform receives algorithmic downranking to maintain fairness
questions.explanation: Preferential attachment means that wealth, credit, or connections are distributed such that those who already have more continue to receive more — 'rich get richer' or the Matthew effect. This is the mechanism that generates hubs in scale-free networks, not a regulatory or fairness concept.

questions.question: Albert, Barabasi, and Jeong estimated that the 'diameter' of the world-wide web is approximately:
options: 19 clicks
6 clicks
100 clicks
50 clicks
questions.explanation: The estimated diameter of the web is 19 clicks — meaning two randomly chosen documents are on average 19 clicks apart. This is distinct from Milgram's 6 degrees of separation in social networks. The key insight is that considerable growth of the web increases this by only one or two clicks.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a scale-free network?
options: A fully random Erdős–Rényi graph with uniform degree distribution
The world-wide web
Most social networks
Some metabolic processes
questions.explanation: A fully random Erdős–Rényi graph has a Poisson (approximately normal) degree distribution, not a power-law. Scale-free networks — defined by power-law degree distributions and preferential attachment — include the web, social networks, and metabolic processes (all cited in the course material).

questions.question: What does the 'constant distance' property of scale-free networks imply for the growth of the web?
options: Considerable growth in web size will only increase the diameter by one or two clicks
All nodes remain equidistant from the central hub regardless of network size
Distance between nodes decreases proportionally as the network grows
The 19-click diameter is fixed permanently and cannot change
questions.explanation: Despite exponential growth of the web, the diameter increases only marginally (by one or two clicks). This is a property of scale-free networks where new hubs absorb most new connections, keeping the overall path length short. It does not mean distance is fixed or decreases proportionally.

questions.question: Scale-free networks govern which type of technology adoption?
options: Network-based digital technologies with preferential attachment dynamics
Linear adoption technologies where each user has an equal probability of adopting
Technologies governed by top-down mandates and regulatory requirements
Hardware technologies with fixed compatibility standards
questions.explanation: The course specifically cites 'some forms of technology adoption, notably the network-based digital technologies' as examples of scale-free networks. This is because adoption follows preferential attachment: popular platforms attract more users, reinforcing their dominance.

questions.question: A network effect is defined as the phenomenon where:
options: The value a user derives from a product depends on the number of users of compatible products
Platform prices increase as more users join, reflecting growing scarcity of network resources
Regulatory bodies intervene to limit monopolistic behavior in digital markets
Algorithmic recommendation engines amplify popular content over niche content
questions.explanation: Network effects (also called demand-side economies of scale) occur when a user's utility from a product grows as more users adopt compatible products. This is a social mutual influence phenomenon, not a price mechanism (option B) or regulatory intervention (option C).

questions.question: The hardware-software paradigm in network economics refers to:
options: The value of a good depending also on the availability of compatible additional goods
The technical relationship between processing power and software complexity
The legal framework separating hardware manufacturers from software developers
A pricing strategy where hardware is sold at a loss and software at a premium
questions.explanation: The hardware-software paradigm holds that the value of a good (hardware) depends on the foreseen utility of compatible additional goods (software). Examples: a computer's value depends on available software; a DVD player's value depends on available movies. Option D (razor/blade model) is a related but distinct pricing strategy.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a main characteristic of industries displaying network properties (Shy Oz)?
options: Diminishing returns to scale in production
Complementarity, compatibility, and standards
Consumption externalities (network effects)
Switching costs and lock-in
questions.explanation: Shy Oz identifies four characteristics: (i) complementarity/compatibility/standards, (ii) consumption externalities, (iii) switching costs and lock-in, and (iv) significant economies of SCALE in production. Diminishing returns — the opposite — is not a characteristic of these markets.

questions.question: Iansiti and Lakhani (2017) describe an additional challenge posed by economic hubs in the digital world as:
options: Hub firms use network assets scaled in one industry to enter and re-architect other industries
Hub firms tend to reduce innovation because their market dominance discourages R&D investment
Hub firms are required by law to share their network infrastructure with competitors
Hub firms lose competitive advantage once their network effects plateau
questions.explanation: Iansiti and Lakhani (2017) argue that hub firms take network-based assets already at scale in one setting and use them to enter another industry and re-architect its structure. This 'platform expansion' dynamic is distinct from innovation disincentives or legal sharing requirements.

questions.question: Which company is cited as the dominant player in internet search as an example of a 'economic hub'?
options: Google
Microsoft
Yahoo
Amazon
questions.explanation: Google is cited as the dominant player (economic hub) in internet search, Facebook in social media, and Amazon in e-commerce. These examples illustrate how network properties and economies of scale lead to the emergence of large players.

questions.question: Which of the following industries is NOT listed as displaying network properties by the course material (citing Shy Oz)?
options: Pharmaceutical research
Telephone services
Computer software
Airline services
questions.explanation: The course lists telephone, e-mail, internet, computer hardware, computer software, music players/titles, video players/movies, banking services, airline services, and legal services as industries displaying network properties. Pharmaceutical research is not among them.

questions.question: When Facebook acquired WhatsApp (2014), Instagram (2012), and Waze (2013), this strategy is best described as:
options: Using network-based assets as strategic assets to eliminate or absorb potential competitors
Vertical integration to control the hardware and software supply chain
A regulatory compliance strategy to meet EU digital market requirements
A diversification strategy into unrelated business sectors
questions.explanation: These acquisitions exemplify the course's discussion of networks as strategic assets — dominant players (hubs) acquire potential competitors to consolidate their network-based advantages. The US House inquiry specifically cited this pattern as anti-competitive (snuffing out competitors through strategic acquisitions).

questions.question: What does 'compliance' mean as a form of social influence?
options: Publicly agreeing with a group while privately maintaining a different opinion
Genuinely adopting the beliefs of a group as one's own internal values
Following orders from an authority figure under fear of punishment
Spreading beliefs through propaganda and systematic media control
questions.explanation: Compliance is surface-level conformity — publicly agreeing to meet social demands while privately holding different views. Internalization (option B) involves genuinely adopting group beliefs. Obedience (option C) involves following authority. Propaganda (option D) is a form of manipulation.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: According to Dominique Cardon's framework, measuring 'authority' on the web is done:
options: From above the web, using links (e.g., Google PageRank, Wikipedia)
From the side of the web, using clicks and visits (e.g., Google Analytics)
From within the web, using likes (e.g., Facebook, Twitter retweets)
From below the web, using traces (e.g., cookies, purchase history)
questions.explanation: Cardon's framework maps measurement position to what is measured: Above = links → authority (PageRank); Side = visits/clicks → popularity; Within = likes → reputation; Below = traces/cookies → predictability. Each position uses different units and underlying principles.

questions.question: In Cardon's framework, measures 'from the side of the web' (e.g., Médiamétrie, Google Analytics) measure:
options: Popularity, using visits and clicks as the unit of measure
Authority, using incoming links as the unit of measure
Reputation, using likes and shares as the unit of measure
Predictability, using cookies and purchase history as the unit of measure
questions.explanation: Measures from the side of the web measure audience popularity. The unit is visits/clicks, and the underlying principle is 'vote.' This contrasts with above (links → authority), within (likes → reputation), and below (traces → predictability).

questions.question: In Cardon's framework, Amazon's recommendation engine operates 'from below the web' because it:
options: Uses traces of past behavior (cookies, purchases) to predict and influence future actions
Ranks products by the number of inbound links from other websites
Measures audience popularity through unique visitor counts and page views
Applies social influence by counting likes and shares from user communities
questions.explanation: 'Below the web' measures the past in order to influence the future, using traces (cookies, purchases) and machine learning (programmability). Amazon's recommendation engine exemplifies this: it predicts the user's next action based on history of past behavior and patterns from other users.

questions.question: Measures 'from within the web' (Facebook, Twitter retweets) measure which quality?
options: Reputation, with likes as the unit of measure and benchmarking as the underlying principle
Authority, with incoming links as the unit of measure and ranking as the underlying principle
Popularity, with clicks as the unit of measure and voting as the underlying principle
Predictability, with behavioral traces as the unit of measure
questions.explanation: Within the web measures reputation through likes/retweets, with benchmarking as the underlying principle. Authority (above, links, ranking), popularity (side, clicks, vote), and predictability (below, traces, programmability) each correspond to a different position in Cardon's framework.

questions.question: Shoshana Zuboff's concept of 'surveillance capitalism' refers to:
options: The commodification of personal behavioral data at scale for purposes of prediction and behavioral modification
State-sponsored mass surveillance programs targeting political dissidents
The voluntary sharing of personal data in exchange for free digital services
Legal frameworks that permit governments to access user data held by platforms
questions.explanation: Surveillance capitalism (Zuboff) refers to the mass collection and commodification of personal data by platforms — not primarily by states. It raises concerns about who owns data, who benefits from it, and the 'division of learning' between data producers and those who exploit that data commercially.

questions.question: Zuboff's 'division of learning' concept refers to:
options: The barrier between those who can access and benefit from data and those who merely produce it
The gap in digital literacy between developed and developing countries
The difference in learning rates between human workers and AI systems
The unequal distribution of educational resources in the digital economy
questions.explanation: 'Division of learning' (Zuboff) is the notion that data producers (users) face a barrier to accessing, understanding, and benefiting from the data they generate, while platforms and companies exploit it. It is a power asymmetry concept, not about geographic inequality or AI learning rates.

questions.question: The principle of 'Who decides who decides?' in Zuboff's framework relates to:
options: The balance of knowledge, authority, and power in the digital economy
Democratic procedures for electing technology regulators
Platform governance models for moderating user-generated content
The technical architecture of distributed ledger systems
questions.explanation: Zuboff's three questions — Who knows? Who decides? Who decides who decides? — address the balance of knowledge, authority, and power in the digital economy. It is a meta-governance question: beyond who makes decisions, who has the power to determine the decision-making structure itself.

questions.question: The statement 'When it's free for you, you become the product' reflects which finding about the digital economy?
options: There is no free lunch: free services are monetized through collection and exploitation of user data
Open-source software is inherently less secure than proprietary paid alternatives
Users who pay for digital services receive stronger privacy protections
Advertising-funded platforms provide worse user experience than subscription models
questions.explanation: This statement encapsulates the core insight: platforms that appear free monetize user data and attention. It is one of the key 'implications of measuring the web' (Summary 1, point 1). The other options introduce comparative claims not made in the course material.

questions.question: The attention economy arises because:
options: In a world of information abundance, human attention becomes scarce and therefore valuable
Digital platforms generate more revenue per user when they capture longer viewing sessions
Cognitive science has proven that humans can focus on at most three simultaneous information streams
Network effects make it profitable to maximize the number of advertisements per page view
questions.explanation: The attention economy concept is based on the scarcity principle: when information becomes abundant (a direct consequence of network society), human attention — the capacity to process that information — becomes the scarce and valuable resource. Options B, C, D are consequences or related business practices, not the root cause.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: In the attention economy, the 'delegation of agency' refers to:
options: The progressive transfer of decision-making and filtering capacity from humans to algorithmic platforms
The formal legal authorization given to AI systems to act on behalf of corporations
The outsourcing of content moderation to third-party contractors
The granting of data access rights from individual users to regulatory authorities
questions.explanation: As platforms filter, organize, and process information on our behalf, they become more autonomous and 'intelligent.' This represents a delegation of agency from the human to the machine — a central concern connecting the attention economy to broader questions of human vs. algorithmic agency.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: An echo chamber is characterized by:
options: An environment where participants encounter only beliefs that reinforce their preexisting views, insulated from rebuttal
A social network in which all members have identical connection patterns
A platform algorithm that randomly distributes content across all user segments
A regulatory framework that enforces balanced content presentation on social media
questions.explanation: An echo chamber is an environment that amplifies existing beliefs through repetition within a closed system, shielded from opposing views. It functions by circulating existing views — the opposite of a balanced content system (option D) or random distribution (option C).
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: 'Confirmation bias' as a reinforcing mechanism in echo chambers refers to:
options: Sharing only content that confirms the preexisting beliefs of a community, reinforcing the credibility of certain information
The algorithmic suppression of content that contradicts mainstream scientific consensus
Users deliberately seeking out opposing viewpoints to validate their own position
Platform A/B testing that gradually adjusts content based on user engagement metrics
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias in the context of echo chambers means sharing only certain types of content within a community of like-minded users, reinforcing the perceived credibility of that content (e.g., 'The world is flat'). It is a user-level cognitive bias amplified by platform design, not an algorithmic suppression mechanism.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: 'Recommendation bias' as a reinforcing mechanism refers to:
options: Algorithms that privilege transgressive or extreme content because it generates higher engagement
A tendency for users to prefer recommendations from friends over algorithmic suggestions
The systematic underrepresentation of minority viewpoints in search results
Platform policies that require equal representation of all political viewpoints
questions.explanation: Recommendation bias means algorithms favor transgressive or sensationalist content (e.g., 'The world is flat') because such content generates more engagement — clicks, shares, time on site. This is a platform design effect that amplifies extreme views, not a user preference or regulatory requirement.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: Which of the three limits of human attention states that 'focus acts as a filter'?
options: Attention is volatile
Perception is subjective
Memory is fallible
Judgment is biased
questions.explanation: The three limits are: (1) Perception is subjective — the world is a construction of our brain; (2) Memory is fallible — we cannot always remember accurately; (3) Attention is volatile — focus acts as a filter. 'Judgment is biased' is not listed as one of the three limits in the course.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: 'Dark patterns' in digital design are best described as:
options: UX design techniques that divert users from their intended goals to serve platform interests
Security vulnerabilities in dark web platforms used for illegal transactions
Visual design choices that reduce readability for users with visual impairments
Algorithmic techniques that detect and remove harmful content from platforms
questions.explanation: Dark patterns are UX design techniques that game designers (and other digital designers) use to divert users — e.g., to make in-app purchases harder to avoid or to trigger addictive behaviors — serving platform interests at the expense of user autonomy. This is distinct from cybersecurity vulnerabilities or accessibility issues.
questions.category: Attention Economy, Echo Chambers, Social Influence

questions.question: Jean Tirole identifies 'information asymmetry between firms and consumers' as a reason for market regulation. Which example best illustrates this in a digital context?
options: Users being unable to determine how their personal data is collected and monetized by platforms
Governments using classified information to regulate technology companies without public scrutiny
Developers having less technical knowledge than platform operators about API design
Investors lacking access to financial data about early-stage tech startups
questions.explanation: Information asymmetry in digital markets arises primarily when users cannot evaluate the full extent of data collection and monetization by platforms — they cannot make fully informed choices. This maps to Tirole's reason #3 (information asymmetry) and connects directly to surveillance capitalism concerns.

questions.question: The AT&T antitrust case (1984) resulted in:
options: The breakup of American Telephone & Telegraph into 7 regional Bell operating companies and long-distance AT&T
Microsoft being forced not to bundle Internet Explorer with Windows
Google being fined for antitrust violations in internet search
Facebook being ordered to divest WhatsApp by the European Commission
questions.explanation: United States v. AT&T (1984) broke up the old AT&T into 7 regional Bell operating companies (RBOCs) and a long-distance AT&T. Microsoft's IE case (option B) was from 1994; Google EU fines (option C) are more recent; Facebook/WhatsApp (option D) is a different proceeding.

questions.question: The EU GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), in force from May 2018, gives individuals:
options: More control over their personal data and establishes one set of data protection rules for all companies operating in the EU
The right to receive compensation from platforms for every byte of personal data collected
Full ownership rights over all data generated through their digital interactions
The ability to opt out of algorithmic recommendation entirely on all platforms
questions.explanation: The GDPR establishes one set of data protection rules across the EU (regardless of company location) and gives people more control over their personal data. It does not provide monetary compensation per byte (option B), full ownership (option C is broader than GDPR's actual provisions), or a guaranteed algorithmic opt-out (option D).

questions.question: The Digital Markets Act (DMA, 2023) specifically targets which type of company?
options: The largest digital platforms operating in the EU, designated as 'gatekeepers'
All technology companies with more than 500 employees operating in the EU
Social media platforms with more than 1 million monthly active users
Companies providing cloud computing services to EU public administrations
questions.explanation: The DMA targets the largest digital platforms in the EU designated as 'gatekeepers' due to their durable market position. In September 2023, 22 services across six companies (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft) were named. The threshold is not simply employee count or user numbers.

questions.question: The Digital Services Act (DSA, 2023) primarily addresses:
options: Content moderation practices and illegal/harmful content (hate speech, counterfeit goods) on online platforms
The pricing of digital services and protection from unfair commercial practices
Data sharing obligations between EU public bodies and private companies
The regulation of artificial intelligence systems in high-risk applications
questions.explanation: The DSA governs content moderation on social media platforms, addressing illegal content, hate speech, and counterfeit goods. Pricing and market contestability is the DMA's domain; data sharing with public bodies is separate; AI regulation falls under the AI Act.

questions.question: Under the EU AI Act, which category of AI usage is explicitly forbidden?
options: Unacceptable risk uses, such as neuro-behavioral manipulation of vulnerable people and real-time biometric ID systems
High risk uses, such as AI in planes, toys, cars, and public infrastructure
Limited risk generative AI, which requires transparency obligations only
Open-source AI models, which are exempt from all risk classifications
questions.explanation: The AI Act defines Unacceptable Risk as forbidden, including neuro-behavioral manipulation of vulnerable people (e.g., voice-activated toys encouraging hazardous behavior), social scoring, and real-time biometric ID systems. High Risk (option B) is regulated but permitted; Limited Risk (option C) requires transparency.

questions.question: The EU Commission's antitrust case against Amazon focused primarily on:
options: Amazon systematically using non-public data from third-party sellers to benefit its own competing retail business
Amazon's refusal to accept payments in EU currencies on its marketplace
Amazon's cloud computing pricing practices discriminating against EU competitors
Amazon's acquisition of a European logistics company blocking domestic competitors
questions.explanation: The EU Commission found Amazon in preliminary breach of antitrust rules for using non-public business data from independent marketplace sellers to benefit Amazon's own retail operations — which directly compete with those sellers. A second investigation also examined preferential treatment for Amazon's logistics services.

questions.question: Which six companies were designated as 'gatekeepers' under the Digital Markets Act in September 2023?
options: Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta, and Microsoft
Google, Facebook, Apple, Twitter, Netflix, and Spotify
Alphabet, Meta, Samsung, Tencent, Amazon, and Oracle
Apple, Microsoft, IBM, Intel, Amazon, and Adobe
questions.explanation: The DMA designated Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta, and Microsoft as gatekeepers in September 2023, with 22 specific services across these six companies. The other options include companies not designated (Twitter/X, Netflix, Tencent, etc.) or exclude ByteDance and Meta.

questions.question: According to the course, one key problem with regulating social media for underage users is:
options: The regulated party (underage young people) is often not the root cause of the harmful consequences that prompted regulation
Social media companies lobby governments to weaken regulations before they are enacted
Young users are the most digitally literate group and thus most able to circumvent restrictions
International law prevents individual countries from restricting access to global platforms
questions.explanation: The course highlights that in the case of social media regulation for minors, the 'regulated party' (underage young people) may not be at the root cause of the harmful consequences — the real drivers may be platform design, algorithmic amplification, or advertiser incentives. This is cited as a problem with regulation.

questions.question: The 'reciprocal influence mechanism' between technology and society means:
options: Technology shapes social relationships while society simultaneously shapes and may hijack technology's purposes
Technology diffuses through society only when endorsed by institutional actors
Social cohesion is a prerequisite for technology adoption in developing economies
Regulatory frameworks must evolve at the same pace as technological innovation
questions.explanation: The reciprocal mechanism has two directions: Technology → Society (distortion of social institutions through massive usage) and Society → Technology (society's 'manyness' shaping usage and potentially hijacking technology from its initial purposes). This bidirectional relationship is a central theme of Class 4.

questions.question: Melvin Kranzberg's first law of technology states that:
options: Technology is neither good nor bad, nor is it neutral
Technology always serves the interests of those who control it
Although technology might be a prime element in many public issues, nontechnical factors take precedence
Every technological advancement generates both a solution and an equivalent new problem
questions.explanation: Kranzberg's first law is 'Technology is neither good nor bad, nor is it neutral.' His fourth law (option C) states that nontechnical factors take precedence in technology-policy decisions. Both are cited in the Class 4 concluding thoughts to emphasize the social embeddedness of technology.

questions.question: Network science, as opposed to network theory, is characterized by:
options: The study of complex real-world networks (biological, social, telecommunication) using interdisciplinary methods from mathematics, physics, and data mining
The formal mathematical study of graphs as representations of abstract relations between discrete objects
The economic analysis of how network effects influence pricing strategies in digital markets
The computational simulation of organizational hierarchies and market structures
questions.explanation: Network science is the interdisciplinary field studying complex real-world networks — drawing on graph theory (mathematics), statistical mechanics (physics), data mining, and computational social science. Network theory (option B) is the more abstract, graph-theoretic foundation. Network economics (option C) is a separate economic sub-field.

questions.question: Network economics refers to:
options: Business economics where value of a good or service increases as more others adopt the same good or service
The study of how internet infrastructure costs are distributed across network providers
Economic models that treat all market participants as equally connected nodes
The branch of economics that studies trade routes and international supply chains
questions.explanation: Network economics refers to business economics benefiting from the network effect: value increases as more users adopt compatible goods or services (e.g., eBay, where community participation drives platform value). This is the demand-side economies of scale concept applied to economic modeling.

questions.question: Computational social science is defined as:
options: The use of computers to model, simulate, and analyze social phenomena, including computational economics and automated analysis of social media content
The application of social science methods to evaluate the societal impact of computing technologies
A branch of computer science focused on building AI systems that can participate in social interactions
The statistical analysis of digital platform usage data for commercial and marketing purposes
questions.explanation: Computational social science uses computers to model, simulate, and analyze social phenomena. It includes computational economics, computational sociology, and automated analysis of social and traditional media. It is social science using computational methods — not the reverse (option B) or purely commercial data analysis (option D).

questions.question: The concept that 'understanding the versatile (multifaceted) nature of technology and its embeddedness in social structures is becoming an increasingly valuable skill' best supports which overall thesis of Class 4?
options: Digital transformation cannot be understood through purely technical lenses; social, cultural, and regulatory factors are equally decisive
Data scientists who specialize in network analysis will command higher salaries than AI engineers
Social media platforms should be required to hire sociologists in addition to engineers
Technical solutions are sufficient to address the harmful consequences of digital technologies
questions.explanation: This concluding statement from Class 4 supports the core thesis that social (non-technical) drivers are integral to understanding digital transformation. Combined with Kranzberg's fourth law ('nontechnical factors take precedence in technology-policy decisions'), it argues for an interdisciplinary approach — not a purely technical or economic one.
